title: Robust and secure programming: validation, authentication and testing

resources.label: Learn C#
resources.note: Our C# practice site. Type each example in, run it, and change it. C# is one of the languages AQA accepts in the exam.

tips.title: Validation is data, authentication is people
tips.body: **Validation** asks *is this data sensible?* **Authentication** asks *are you who you say you are?* Mixing them up is the fastest way to lose a definition mark in this topic.

tips.title: Three kinds of test data
tips.body: **Normal** data that should be accepted, **boundary** data at the very edge of what is allowed, and **erroneous** data that should be rejected. Give a boundary value on **each** side of the limit: for 1 to 6, that is 0, 1, 6 and 7.

tips.title: A loop, not an IF
tips.body: Validation that uses an `IF` checks once and gives up. A `WHILE` loop keeps asking until the input is acceptable, which is what robust means. Reach for the loop.

tips.title: Two error types only
tips.body: AQA recognises **syntax** errors, where the code breaks the language's rules, and **logic** errors, where it runs but does the wrong thing. Dividing by zero counts as a logic error; there is no third category to name.

why.matters:
A program that works is one that works when somebody does the thing you did not think of: typing a word where a number goes, leaving the box empty, entering an age of 400. Code that only handles the sensible case is not finished, it is half tested.

That is what **robust** means, and the specification treats it as three skills — validating input before you trust it, authenticating the person, and testing with data chosen to break things. Each can be examined, including inside a longer programming question that asks for validated input.

examples.title: Why an IF is not enough to check an age
examples.body:
An `IF` looks once. If the age is wrong it prints a message — and then the program carries straight on with the wrong age, which is worse than not checking at all, because now it looks as though it did.

A `WHILE` keeps asking until the answer passes, so every line after the loop can **trust** the value. The condition describes the **bad** input and joins the halves with `OR`: `WHILE age < 11 OR age > 18`. Getting that round the right way is most of the marks, because a condition that describes the good input lets every wrong answer through.

nodes.text: Now the age can be trusted

visual.alt: A flow chart of a validation loop: the age is read, a decision asks whether it is below eleven or above eighteen, the yes branch says so and asks again and returns to the decision, and only the no branch leaves the loop

examples.title: Why a login says "wrong username or password"
examples.body:
It looks unhelpful, and it is deliberate. A message that says *no account with that name* has just told whoever typed it that the name is free — and a message that says *wrong password* has told them the opposite, which is worth far more.

One message for both mistakes gives nothing away. It sits alongside two other good habits, beyond what the specification requires: **limit the attempts** before locking out, so guessing cannot simply be repeated, and store a **hash** of the password rather than the password itself, so a stolen list does not reveal the passwords directly. The specification only asks you to write routines that check a plain-text username and password.

visual.alt: A table of three login failure messages: the vague one tells the user to try again and an attacker nothing, while naming which half was wrong tells an attacker whether an account with that name exists

examples.title: Why the program that runs is the dangerous one
examples.body:
AQA names exactly **two** kinds of error. A **syntax error** breaks the rules of the language — a missing bracket, a misspelt keyword. A compiler will not produce a program at all; an interpreter stops when it reaches the line. Either way the program cannot run past it, the translator reports it for you, and it is the easy kind.

A **logic error** breaks nothing. The program runs, finishes and gives an answer, and the answer is wrong. Nothing will tell you: no message, no crash, no red underline. The only thing that finds a logic error is testing it with data whose right answer you worked out beforehand.

visual.alt: A table of the two kinds of error: a syntax error breaks the rules of the language so the program cannot run past it and the translator reports it, while a logic error runs happily and gives a wrong answer that only testing finds

steps.title: Robust means it does not fall over
steps.body:
A **robust** program copes with anything the user does: wrong types, silly values, empty input. The main tool is **validation**: checking data before using it. AQA's specification names three by example, length, presence and range, and two more are worth knowing:

- **Range**: between two limits, such as an age from 11 to 18.
- **Length**: enough characters, such as a password of at least 8.
- **Presence**: not empty.
- **Type**: a number where a number is expected.
- **Format**: matches a pattern, such as an email with an @.

Validation checks that data is **sensible**, not that it is **true**. A wrong but sensible date of birth passes.

visuals.problem: Choose a check for each input

steps.text: Postcode: format check
Quantity of tickets: range check, 1 to 6
Username: presence check, then a length check
Year of birth: type check (a number), then a range check

check.prompt: A form rejects a phone number because it is only 5 digits long. Which check is this?
check.solution: It is a **length check**: the program is counting the characters and rejecting the input because there are too few, not looking at what those characters are.
options: Presence check
Range check
Length check
Format check

steps.title: Validation in code: a loop, not an IF
steps.body:
An IF can spot bad input once. A **WHILE loop** keeps asking until the input passes, so the code after it can trust the value.

```
age ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
WHILE age < 11 OR age > 18
   OUTPUT 'Enter an age between 11 and 18'
   age ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
ENDWHILE
```

The condition describes the **bad** input, joined with `OR`: too low **or** too high. The loop body prints a message and reads again.

The same loop shape checks **length** and **presence**, the other two checks the specification gives as examples:

```
name ← USERINPUT
WHILE name = '' OR LEN(name) < 5
   OUTPUT 'Enter a username of at least 5 characters'
   name ← USERINPUT
ENDWHILE
```

`name = ''` is the presence check and `LEN(name) < 5` the length check. An empty name has length 0, so the length check alone would also catch it, but writing both makes each check visible.

visuals.alt: Trace of the age validation loop with inputs 9 then 25 then 14

visuals.problem: Trace the username loop when the user presses Enter without typing, then types Al, then Alexa

steps.text: Nothing typed: name = '' is True, so the message is output and the loop asks again
Al: not empty, but LEN is 2 and 2 < 5 is True, so the message is output again
Alexa: not empty, and LEN is 5, so 5 < 5 is False and the loop ends
The message was output 2 times, and name now holds Alexa

check.prompt: The loop condition is written as `age < 11 AND age > 18`. What happens?
check.solution: No number is both below 11 and above 18. The bad-input condition needs OR.
options: The condition can never be true, so no value is ever rejected
The loop runs forever, because the condition is always true
It works exactly the same as OR, so every bad value is rejected
Only ages below 11 are rejected, because that part is checked first

steps.title: Putting validation in a function
steps.body: Validation code is reused, so it belongs in a subroutine that returns the checked value.

visuals.problem: A function that returns a positive number

steps.text:
```
SUBROUTINE get_positive()
   n ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
   WHILE n ≤ 0
      OUTPUT 'Must be positive'
      n ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
   ENDWHILE
   RETURN n
ENDSUBROUTINE
```
The loop repeats while n is 0 or negative
Only a valid n reaches the RETURN, so the caller never sees a bad value
Call it wherever a positive number is needed: size ← get_positive()

check.prompt: With `get_positive`, the user types −3, then 0, then 8. What is returned?
check.solution: −3 and 0 both fail n ≤ 0; 8 passes and is returned.

steps.title: Authentication: who are you?
steps.body:
**Authentication** checks the **person**, usually with a username and password. Good practice, some of it beyond what the specification asks you to write:

- Compare the entered password with the stored one and give the same message for a wrong username as for a wrong password, so an attacker learns nothing.
- **Limit attempts**, then lock out, to stop guessing.
- Real systems do not store passwords as plain text: they store a **hash** and compare hashes. The specification only asks you to write routines with plain-text usernames and passwords.

```
attempts ← 0
OUTPUT 'Password?'
entered ← USERINPUT
WHILE entered ≠ stored AND attempts < 2
   attempts ← attempts + 1
   OUTPUT 'Wrong, try again'
   entered ← USERINPUT
ENDWHILE
IF entered = stored THEN
   OUTPUT 'Welcome'
ELSE
   OUTPUT 'Locked out'
ENDIF
```

The user gets three tries: one before the loop and two inside it.

visuals.alt: Trace of the password loop with three wrong entries

steps.text:
```
OUTPUT 'Username?'
user ← USERINPUT
OUTPUT 'Password?'
pass ← USERINPUT
IF user = storedUser AND pass = storedPass THEN
   OUTPUT 'Welcome'
ELSE
   OUTPUT 'Login failed'
ENDIF
```
Both must match, so the two checks are joined with AND
One message covers both failures, so an attacker cannot tell which half was wrong
AQA asks for plain-text usernames and passwords in code; you will not be asked to write a hash

check.prompt: Which is authentication rather than validation?
check.solution: Password checking identifies the user; the rest check data.
options: Checking a password matches the stored one
Checking an age is between 11 and 18 before allowing signup
Checking a name is not blank
Checking an email contains an @

steps.title: Testing: normal, boundary, erroneous
steps.body:
Before a program is used it is **tested** with three kinds of data, each with an **expected result** written down first:

- **Normal**: typical values that should be accepted. For a mark from 0 to 100: 55.
- **Boundary**: values on the edge. 0 and 100 should be accepted; 101 and −1, just outside, should be rejected.
- **Erroneous**: values that must be rejected: 250, −40, the word "ten".

A test table has columns for the data, the type, the expected result and the actual result.

visuals.alt: A test plan for a mark from 0 to 100, with the actual-result column left blank to fill in once each test has been run

check.prompt: A program accepts a number of players from 2 to 4. Which pair sits on the edge, inside the allowed range?
check.solution: 2 and 4 are the edges inside the range. Full boundary testing also uses 1 and 5, the values just outside, which should be rejected.
options: 2 and 4
3 and 10
0 and 100
3 and 3

steps.title: Syntax errors and logic errors
steps.body:
- A **syntax error** breaks the rules of the language: a missing bracket, a misspelt keyword. A compiler will not produce a program at all; an interpreter stops when it reaches the line. Either way the program cannot run past it.
- A **logic error** lets the program run but gives the **wrong answer**: `<` instead of `≤`, adding in the wrong place. Only testing finds these, and a **trace table** shows where the values first go wrong.
- Some faults make a running program crash: dividing by zero, reading past the end of an array. AQA sorts errors into only two types, **syntax** and **logic**, and a fault like this counts as a logic error because the code obeys the language's rules.

steps.text: OUTPUT 'Hello  (missing quote): syntax error
total / count when count is 0: logic error — the code is legal, the reasoning is wrong, and the program crashes at that line
A discount applied before tax instead of after: logic error

check.prompt: A program is meant to count values above 50 but uses `> 5`. It runs and outputs a number. What kind of error is this?
check.solution: A **logic error**. The program runs without crashing, so it is not a syntax error, but `> 5` counts values above 5 rather than above 50, so the answer it produces is wrong.
options: Erroneous data
Logic error
Syntax error
Not an error, because it ran

steps.title: Your turn: design the tests, then write the check
steps.body:
A program asks how many tickets to book, from 1 to 6. Write a test plan with normal, boundary and erroneous data and the expected result for each. Then write the validation loop.

Build the loop on our [Learn C#](https://red-dune-0f7372e10.7.azurestaticapps.net/) site with `int.TryParse` for the type check and a `while` loop for the range.

steps.text:
```
tickets ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
WHILE tickets < 1 OR tickets > 6
   OUTPUT 'Choose from 1 to 6'
   tickets ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
ENDWHILE
```

Normal: 3. Boundary: 1 and 6 accepted, 0 and 7 rejected. Erroneous: 20, −1, "six". This loop only checks the range: for "six" to be rejected rather than crash the program, a type check is needed before STRING_TO_INT (in C#, int.TryParse)

check.prompt: The user types 7, then 0, then 6. How many times is the message output?
check.solution: 7 and 0 are both rejected with a message; 6 passes. The message is output **2** times.

steps.title: Going deeper: writing the whole thing
steps.body: Longer programming questions often ask for input **with validation**, some processing, and output. Structure first: a subroutine that returns validated input, a loop or calculation, then output. Say what each test in your plan is **for**, and give the boundary values on **both** sides of the edge. When asked about security, name the practice and the attack it stops: attempt limits stop brute-force guessing; storing hashes means a stolen list does not reveal the passwords directly.

visuals.problem: Plan a program: read scores until the user enters −1, reject anything else outside 0 to 100, then output the mean

steps.text: Subroutine get_score() with a loop accepting −1 or 0 to 100
Main loop: total and count until −1
Guard against count = 0 before dividing, then output total / count

check.prompt: Why should the mean program check that count is not 0 before dividing?
check.solution: Guarding the division makes the program robust to the empty case.
options: Zero scores would give a mean of zero, which is a wrong answer that a logic error would produce
Because count is a global variable, and global variables cannot be used in a division
Count is a string and must be converted to a number before it can be used in a division
Dividing by zero makes the program fail at that line, so it would crash if the user entered −1 straight away

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Validation checks data is sensible: range, length, presence, type, format. Use a WHILE loop with the bad-input condition joined by OR.
- Authentication checks identity: compare the username and password with the stored ones. Limiting attempts and storing hashes are good habits beyond what the specification asks you to code.
- Test with normal, boundary and erroneous data, each with an expected result written first.
- Syntax errors stop the program being translated, or running past that line; logic errors let it run and give the wrong answer, and are found by testing and trace tables. AQA examines these two types.
- In a big programming question, structure first: validated input, processing, output.

visuals.alt: A reference table of validation checks, giving for each the question it asks and an example: range, length, presence, type and format

questions.prompt: What is validation?
questions.solution: Validation checks the data. Authentication checks the person.
options: Checking that the user is the person they claim to be before letting them access the system
Converting a string typed by the user into a number the program can use
Checking that input is sensible and in the expected form before the program uses it
Testing a program with typical data to make sure it gives the right answers

questions.prompt: What is authentication?
questions.solution: Authentication is about who, validation is about what.
options: Confirming the identity of a user, for example with a username and password
Checking that a number typed by the user lies within an allowed range, such as 1 to 10
Testing a program with erroneous data before it is released
Making sure every file the program opened has been closed again

questions.prompt: A program asks for a percentage score from 0 to 100. Which of these is boundary test data: 50, 0, 200 or −40? Give the value.
questions.solution: Boundary data sits on the edge of the allowed range or just outside it. Here that is 0; the full boundary set is −1, 0, 100 and 101. 50 is normal; 200 and −40 are erroneous.

questions.prompt: A program crashes when the user types a word instead of a number. What kind of test data was this?
questions.solution: A word where a number is expected is erroneous. A robust program rejects it and asks again.
options: Erroneous data: input the program should reject
Normal data: typical input
Boundary data: an edge case at the limit that is allowed
Valid data that was entered too quickly

questions.prompt: Which is a range check?
questions.solution: Range checks test between limits. The others are length, format and presence checks.
options: Rejecting a password shorter than 8 characters
Rejecting an empty name
Rejecting an email address with no @ symbol
Rejecting an age that is below 11 or above 18

questions.prompt: What validation check rejects a postcode that does not match the pattern of letters and numbers expected?
questions.solution: A format check compares the input with a pattern. Length, range, presence and type are the others.

questions.prompt: Explain why a program that reads a number should use a loop for validation rather than a single IF statement.
questions.solution: So the program keeps asking until the input is acceptable. A single check can only reject bad input once; a loop repeats the prompt until the value passes, so the program can never continue with data it has already rejected.

markScheme.description: Rest of program has valid data

criteria.text: A single IF rejects the bad input once but does not ask again, so the program continues with no valid value
A loop keeps asking until the input is acceptable
So the rest of the program always works with valid data

questions.modelAnswer: An IF can spot a bad value and print a message, but the program then carries on without a good value. A WHILE loop repeats the request until the value passes the check, so when the loop ends the program is guaranteed to have valid data to work with.

questions.prompt: What is a syntax error?
questions.solution: A syntax error is code that breaks the rules of the language, so it cannot be translated and run: a compiler will not produce a program, and an interpreter stops when it reaches the line. A logic error runs but gives the wrong result.
options: A program that runs all the way through but produces the wrong answer because of a mistake
A test that fails because the tester typed erroneous data instead of normal data
A program that stops part way through because it runs out of memory while it is executing
Code that breaks the language's rules, such as a missing bracket, so it cannot be translated and run

questions.prompt: A program asks for a whole number of tickets between 1 and 6. Give one example of normal data, a pair of boundary values (one on each side of a limit) and one example of erroneous data, and for each say what the program should do.
questions.solution: Three kinds of data, each with the expected behaviour, and the boundary pair on both sides of the edge.

criteria.text: Normal: a value such as 3, accepted and processed
Boundary: 1 or 6, accepted (and 0 or 7 rejected, as boundary values just outside)
Erroneous: a value such as 10, −2 or the word "two", rejected with a message and the question asked again

questions.modelAnswer: Normal: 3, which is accepted and used to book three tickets. Boundary: 1 and 6, the smallest and largest allowed, both accepted; 0 and 7, just outside, both rejected. Erroneous: 10, or −2, or the word two, all rejected with a message, and the program asks again.

questions.prompt: Write a subroutine `get_mark()` that asks the user for a mark, keeps asking until the mark is from 0 to 100, and returns it.
questions.solution: The loop condition must use OR: it repeats when the mark is too low or too high.

criteria.text: Subroutine header and RETURN of the mark
Reads the input and converts it with STRING_TO_INT
WHILE loop with the condition mark < 0 OR mark > 100
Inside the loop an error message and a fresh input
Correct structure: ENDWHILE, ENDSUBROUTINE, no OUTPUT of the mark inside

questions.modelAnswer:
```
SUBROUTINE get_mark()
   mark ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
   WHILE mark < 0 OR mark > 100
      OUTPUT 'Enter a mark from 0 to 100'
      mark ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
   ENDWHILE
   RETURN mark
ENDSUBROUTINE
```

questions.prompt:
In this program `stored` holds the correct password. If the user types the wrong password every time, how many times in total is the user asked to type it?

```
attempts ← 0
OUTPUT 'Password?'
entered ← USERINPUT
WHILE entered ≠ stored AND attempts < 2
   attempts ← attempts + 1
   OUTPUT 'Wrong, try again'
   entered ← USERINPUT
ENDWHILE
IF entered = stored THEN
   OUTPUT 'Welcome'
ELSE
   OUTPUT 'Locked out'
ENDIF
```
questions.solution: Once before the loop, then twice inside it (attempts goes 1 then 2, and the loop stops when attempts reaches 2). **3** attempts in total, then Locked out.

markScheme.description: One input before the loop and the loop runs twice

questions.prompt: Why is limiting password attempts a good security measure?
questions.solution: Three tries then lock out defeats guessing at scale.
options: It makes the password longer each time, so an attacker has to guess more characters on every attempt
It means the password does not need to be stored, because the program only remembers the number of tries
It stops an attacker trying thousands of guesses in a row, so a brute-force attack on the password is not practical
It makes the program run faster, because it checks fewer passwords before deciding to lock the user out

questions.prompt:
What kind of error does this program contain, and when is it found?

```
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 3
   total ← total + i
ENDFOR
count ← 0
OUTPUT total / count
```
questions.solution: AQA's specification names two types of error: syntax and logic. This code is legal, so it starts running; the fault is in the reasoning, which makes it a logic error. The program crashes at the last line, but AQA sorts errors into only two types, and this one is a logic error.

markScheme.description: Logic error, found when the line runs

options: No error at all: the program runs to the end, the loop adds 1, 2 and 3 correctly, and the output is the total of 6
An error in the FOR loop: it adds 1 to 3 when the question needs 1 to 4, so the total is wrong before the last line runs
A syntax error: dividing by zero breaks the rules of the language, so the program is rejected before it starts and nothing at all is output
A logic error: the code obeys the rules of the language so it runs, but dividing by zero is a mistake in the reasoning and the program fails at that line

questions.prompt: A student writes a program that calculates the average of three test scores but always outputs a value that is too small. Explain what kind of error this is and describe how a trace table would help find it.
questions.solution: Name the error type, say what the trace table records, say how it locates the line.

markScheme.description: First wrong value locates the line

criteria.text: It is a logic error: the program runs without crashing but gives the wrong result
A trace table records the value of every variable after each line
Comparing the traced values with the expected values shows the first line where they differ, which is where the mistake is, for example dividing before adding or dividing by the wrong number

questions.modelAnswer: The program runs and produces a number, so it is not a syntax error: it is a logic error. Tracing the program in a table, line by line, records what each variable holds. Comparing those values with what they should be shows exactly the first line where the value goes wrong, for example a total that is missing one score or a division by 4 instead of 3, and that line is where the fix goes.

questions.prompt: A website stores passwords. Which is the most secure approach among these?
questions.solution: Storing a hash means someone who steals the file does not get the passwords directly. The others are readable or reversible. AQA only requires you to write authentication with plain text usernames and passwords, so you will not have to code a hash; knowing why a stored hash is safer than the password itself is useful background beyond the specification.
options: Store the passwords in a text file that only the website can read
Store a hash of each password and compare hashes, so the real passwords are never stored
Email each user their password so it need not be stored
Store the passwords in reverse so they cannot be read directly

questions.prompt:
This program should output the larger of two numbers, but it always outputs the smaller one.

```
1 a ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
2 b ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
3 IF a > b THEN
4    OUTPUT b
5 ELSE
6    OUTPUT a
7 ENDIF
```

Give the number of the first line that must be changed.
questions.solution: Line 3's test is right; the outputs are swapped. Line 4 should be OUTPUT a and line 6 should be OUTPUT b, so line 4 is the first that must change. This is a logic error: the program runs and gives the wrong answer. Changing line 3 to `IF a < b THEN` instead also fixes the program, so 3 is accepted as well.

markScheme.description: Line 4; accept line 3 if the test is reversed to `IF a < b THEN`

questions.prompt: A program accepts a password of at least 8 characters. Give one item of **boundary** test data and justify why you chose it.
questions.solution: Name the data, say which kind it is, and say what mistake it would catch.

markScheme.description: A named item of test data

criteria.text: A named item of test data, such as a password of exactly 8 characters or of 7 characters
Its type identified: boundary — exactly 8 characters (the shortest accepted) or 7 (just below, rejected)
The justification: it checks the program accepts or rejects correctly right at the limit, which is where an off-by-one mistake in the length check would show up

questions.modelAnswer: A password of exactly 7 characters, such as "abcdefg". It is boundary data, one character below the shortest allowed length. It checks that the program rejects a password just under the limit, which is exactly where an off-by-one error in the length check (using < 7 instead of < 8) would let a bad password through. A password of exactly 8 characters is boundary data too: it checks that the shortest allowed password is accepted.

questions.prompt:
The user types `cat`, then `letmein`, then `letmein1` into this program. How many times is `Too short` output?

```
pwd ← USERINPUT
WHILE LEN(pwd) < 8
   OUTPUT 'Too short'
   pwd ← USERINPUT
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT 'Saved'
```
questions.solution: cat has 3 characters and letmein has 7, so both make `LEN(pwd) < 8` True and each is followed by the message. letmein1 has 8 characters, 8 < 8 is False, and the loop ends. `Too short` is output **2** times.

questions.prompt: A program accepts a username only if it has at least 5 characters. Which pair of usernames is boundary test data for this check?
questions.solution: Boundary data sits at the limit and just the other side of it: usernames of 4 and 5 characters. The shortest allowed username has 5 characters and should be accepted; 4 characters is just below it and should be rejected. An empty username is erroneous data, and usernames of 8, 10 or 50 characters are normal data for this check.
options: Usernames of 1 and 50 characters
Usernames of 4 and 5 characters
An empty username and one of 8 characters
Usernames of 5 and 10 characters

questions.prompt:
A login is written like this:

```
user ← USERINPUT
pass ← USERINPUT
IF user = storedUser OR pass = storedPass THEN
   OUTPUT 'Welcome'
ELSE
   OUTPUT 'Login failed'
ENDIF
```

What is wrong with it?
questions.solution: OR is True when either side is True, so someone who knows only the username or only the password gets in: the right username with any password at all gives Welcome. Both must match, so the condition needs AND: `IF user = storedUser AND pass = storedPass THEN`. A user who types both correctly is still let in, which is why testing only with the right details would never find this logic error.

markScheme.description: OR lets in someone who knows only one of the two

options: Nothing is wrong: OR checks that both the username and password are correct
It turns away a user who types both of them correctly
Someone who knows only the username or only the password gets in
USERINPUT cannot be compared with a value that is stored

questions.prompt: Write an algorithm that keeps asking the user for a username until it is not empty and has at least 5 characters. Output a message each time a username is rejected, then output `Username saved` once one is accepted.
questions.solution: Read once before the loop, loop while the input is bad, re-read inside the loop, and only output once the loop has ended. A REPEAT … UNTIL loop whose condition describes the good input works as well.

markScheme.description: Message and fresh input inside the loop
Output after the loop, correct structure

criteria.text: Reads the username with USERINPUT before the loop (not needed with REPEAT … UNTIL, which reads inside)
A loop condition that rejects both faults: WHILE name = '' OR LEN(name) < 5 (LEN(name) < 5 alone also catches an empty name), or REPEAT … UNTIL name ≠ '' AND LEN(name) ≥ 5
Inside the loop, a message saying the username was rejected and a fresh USERINPUT
After the loop, outputs Username saved; correct structure with ENDWHILE or UNTIL

questions.modelAnswer:
```
name ← USERINPUT
WHILE name = '' OR LEN(name) < 5
   OUTPUT 'Enter a username of at least 5 characters'
   name ← USERINPUT
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT 'Username saved'
```

`name = ''` is the presence check and `LEN(name) < 5` the length check. The condition describes the **bad** input and joins the two with OR, so the loop only ends when the name passes both.

questions.prompt: The correct username is held in `storedUser` and the correct password in `storedPass`, both as plain text. Write an authentication routine that asks for a username and a password, allows up to three attempts, outputs `Welcome` as soon as both match, and outputs `Locked out` after three failed attempts.
questions.solution: A counter and a flag before the loop; inside it, read both values and check them together with AND; count each failure; stop on a match or after three failures; then output the result once.

markScheme.description: Counter (and flag) set up before the loop
Both values read inside the loop
Counter increased for each failed attempt
Loop ends on a match or after three failures
Welcome or Locked out output correctly

criteria.text: An attempt counter set to 0 before the loop, and a flag such as loggedIn ← False if one is used
Asks for the username and the password with USERINPUT inside the loop, so every attempt reads both again (a first read before the loop is fine)
Checks both at once: user = storedUser AND pass = storedPass, or the same test inverted in a loop condition: user ≠ storedUser OR pass ≠ storedPass
Adds 1 to the counter for each failed attempt (or for each attempt)

The loop stops after a match or after three attempts: WHILE attempts < 3 AND NOT loggedIn, REPEAT … UNTIL loggedIn OR attempts = 3, or, after one read before the loop, WHILE (user ≠ storedUser OR pass ≠ storedPass) AND attempts < 2
Outputs Welcome after a match and Locked out only after three failures, with correct structure

questions.modelAnswer:
```
attempts ← 0
loggedIn ← False
WHILE attempts < 3 AND NOT loggedIn
   OUTPUT 'Username?'
   user ← USERINPUT
   OUTPUT 'Password?'
   pass ← USERINPUT
   IF user = storedUser AND pass = storedPass THEN
      loggedIn ← True
   ELSE
      attempts ← attempts + 1
      OUTPUT 'Wrong username or password'
   ENDIF
ENDWHILE
IF loggedIn THEN
   OUTPUT 'Welcome'
ELSE
   OUTPUT 'Locked out'
ENDIF
```

Three wrong attempts make `attempts` 3 and the loop ends with `loggedIn` still False, so the output is Locked out. A match on the second attempt sets `loggedIn` to True and the loop ends straight away, so the output is Welcome.

The lesson's pattern earns the same marks:

```
attempts ← 0
user ← USERINPUT
pass ← USERINPUT
WHILE (user ≠ storedUser OR pass ≠ storedPass) AND attempts < 2
   attempts ← attempts + 1
   OUTPUT 'Wrong username or password'
   user ← USERINPUT
   pass ← USERINPUT
ENDWHILE
IF user = storedUser AND pass = storedPass THEN
   OUTPUT 'Welcome'
ELSE
   OUTPUT 'Locked out'
ENDIF
```

examTechnique.body: These ideas appear in three places: short definitions (validation, authentication, the two error types), test-plan questions (normal, boundary, erroneous with expected results), and inside a longer programming question that asks for validated input. Use the specification words and give the boundary values on both sides of the edge.
examinerErrors: Confusing validation (is the data sensible?) with authentication (is this the right person?).
Writing a validation condition with AND when it needs OR.
Giving only one boundary value, or none just outside the range.
Calling a logic error a syntax error because the answer was wrong.
Describing test data without saying what the program should do with it.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the right check for each input, writes validation as a loop in a function that returns the value, plans tests with expected results on both sides of every boundary, classifies errors by when they appear, and links each security practice to the attack it prevents.
